strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of invariant prediction: an otherwise reliable feature may be missing or occluded at test time. The SIL formulation and H-CMNIST benchmark make reliance on multiple invariant cues an explicit research objective relevant to visual recognition.

The reported experiments demonstrate practical value across diverse distribution shifts. ASGDRO improves CelebA worst-group accuracy from GDRO’s 87.2% to 91.0%, FMoW performance from 30.8% to 35.0%, and DomainBed average accuracy from ERM’s 63.3% to 65.9%. Acceptance need not depend on leading every individual benchmark.

H-CMNIST provides useful controlled evidence of improved shape utilization after removing color. With the spurious box retained, ASGDRO achieves 66.62% versus GDRO’s 57.53%. Comparisons against both ASAM and GDRO help establish the benefit of combining their ingredients.

The approach integrates with existing methods: adding ASGDRO to DPLCLIP increases average accuracy from 72.6% to 74.0%. Clear motivating illustrations, a code link, and appendix details covering group definitions, hyperparameter searches, repeated runs, and validation protocols support understanding and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect as stated, undermining a central claimed contribution. Appendix A.4 explicitly uses R(theta)=0.5(Y−sum_i theta_i)^2. Taking Y=1 and theta=lambda on the probability simplex gives max_{||epsilon||_2≤rho} R(lambda+epsilon)=rho^2 p/2 for every lambda. Thus a single-feature solution and uniform feature weights have identical robust risk; the objective does not select balanced weights. The proof introduces a lambda-dependent gradient factor without justification. This substantive correctness issue is the main reason my recommendation favors weak rejection despite the empirical merits.

The broader connection between SIL and parameter-space flatness remains heuristic. Section 3.3 equates the maximum risk over individual invariant mechanisms with the maximum over an entire parameter ball. Low loss along interpolation paths does not establish this equality or low loss throughout that ball. Likewise, Proposition 1’s first-order gradient penalty does not establish flatness at stationary points, where gradients vanish regardless of curvature. These gaps affect the proposed scientific explanation.

The evaluated algorithm differs materially from the analyzed objective. Section 3.5 states that all experiments except the toy example use one perturbation computed from the mean-risk gradient, while Equation (3) and Algorithm 1 use separate adversarial perturbations for each environment. Environment gradients can cancel or disagree, so the shared perturbation need not expose each environment’s sharp directions. No comparison or approximation bound establishes that this substitution preserves the claimed mechanism; the adaptive perturbation geometry also differs from the theorem’s Euclidean ball.

The experiments establish predictive improvements more strongly than the claimed feature-sufficiency mechanism. H-CMNIST supplies the only direct missing-invariant-feature intervention. The real-image experiments measure ordinary distribution-shift performance, while broader Grad-CAM activation and smaller Hessian eigenvalues do not establish use of multiple independently predictive cues. Consequently, the empirical evidence does not resolve the theoretical gaps supporting the manuscript’s stronger guarantees.

There are also correctable reporting and reproducibility issues. Table 3 reports RxRx1 accuracy of 32.2±0.2%, whereas Figure 7 reports 30.5±0.1%, without explaining the difference. Appendix A.8 provides limited dataset-specific training details, and the efficiency and sensitivity analyses advertised in Section 4.3 are not supplied. These are secondary concerns rather than the primary basis for rejection.
